about: A bartender is called Mark, and the book also holds 'a mark on the wall', 'the guild's mark' and a sentence-initial imperative 'Mark the spot'; the name is one man, the common word is no recurring term.
title: The Back Room
author: Ada Pell

chapters.title: Closing
paragraphs: Mark wiped the counter and hung the cloth over the tap. He did it every night at the same minute.
There was a mark on the wall behind the bar, a long grey smear at shoulder height. Nobody remembered how it had got there.
Lorna came in out of the rain and shook her coat. She asked for the usual and Mark poured it without a word.
Mark leaned on the bar. He liked the hour when the room was still empty.
The mark on the wall had been there longer than the bar itself. The owner swore it was a burn from the old fire.
Lorna drank slowly and watched the door. She had the look of someone who expected a letter.
Mark polished a glass against the light. He held it up and found a spot and polished it again.
"Mark the spot," said a drunk in the corner, pointing at the ceiling. Nobody asked what spot he meant.
A man came in with a leather satchel and a stiff collar. Mark looked at him once and put down the glass.
Lorna turned her stool toward the stranger. She said she did not know him.
The stranger laid a coin on the bar, stamped with the guild's mark. Mark did not touch it.
Mark said the house did not take that kind of money. He said it quietly, as he said everything.
The stranger smiled and put the coin away. He asked about the mark on the wall instead.
Mark told him it was an old burn. Lorna said it was a hand, and that she could see the fingers.
They looked at the wall for a long moment. In the lamplight the mark did look a little like a hand.
The stranger finished his drink and left. Mark locked the door behind him and drew the bolt.
Lorna stayed until midnight. Mark washed the last glass and turned down the lamp.
In the morning Mark found a new mark on the wall, small and neat, at the height of a child's hand.
In the district everyone knew Mark, and nobody had a bad word for Mark.
Years afterwards people still asked about Mark, though few could say why.
In the district everyone knew Lorna, and nobody had a bad word for Lorna.
Years afterwards people still asked about Lorna, though few could say why.
